questions.question: What is the pretraining objective for decoder-only transformer LLMs like GPT and Claude?
options: Predicting randomly masked tokens in the middle of a sentence (like BERT)
Classifying documents into predefined categories
Predicting the next token given all preceding tokens (autoregressive language modeling)
Translating text between two languages
questions.explanation: Decoder-only LLMs are trained with autoregressive language modeling: given tokens x_1 through x_{t-1}, predict x_t. This is applied to every position simultaneously using causal masking. Despite its simplicity, this objective at massive scale produces models with broad language understanding and generation capabilities.

questions.question: Why do modern LLMs use subword tokenization (like BPE) instead of word-level tokenization?
options: Subword tokenization produces shorter sequences, making transformers faster
It balances vocabulary size and sequence length while eliminating the out-of-vocabulary problem -- any text can be represented as a sequence of subword tokens
Word-level tokenization is not supported by PyTorch
Subword tokenization always produces exactly one token per word
questions.explanation: Word-level tokenization requires a massive vocabulary and cannot handle unseen words. Character-level tokenization creates very long sequences (expensive for O(n^2) attention). BPE and similar subword methods find a middle ground: common words stay as single tokens while rare words are split into frequent subword pieces, ensuring any text can be tokenized.

questions.question: What do scaling laws tell us about LLM training?
options: Larger models always perform better regardless of training data size
Model performance improves predictably with more parameters and data, following power laws, and model size and data size should be scaled together
There is a fixed maximum model size beyond which no improvement is possible
Scaling only affects training speed, not model quality
questions.explanation: Scaling laws (Kaplan et al., Hoffmann et al.) show that loss decreases as a power law in both model size N and data size D. Critically, the Chinchilla scaling laws showed that compute-optimal training requires scaling both together -- roughly 20 tokens per parameter. This means a 10B parameter model should see about 200B tokens.

questions.question: What is the purpose of RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)?
options: To teach the model basic language understanding
To reduce the model's parameter count for faster inference
To align the model's behavior with human preferences, making it more helpful and less harmful, beyond what supervised fine-tuning alone achieves
To enable the model to process images in addition to text
questions.explanation: After pretraining (which produces a raw text predictor) and SFT (which teaches assistant-like formatting), RLHF further refines the model by training it to produce outputs that humans prefer. A reward model learned from human comparisons guides the optimization, pushing the model toward responses that are more helpful, accurate, and safe.

questions.question: How does LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) make fine-tuning more efficient?
options: It removes unnecessary layers from the model
It freezes the original model weights and adds small trainable low-rank matrices (with rank r << d), training less than 1% of total parameters
It converts the model from float32 to int8 precision
It fine-tunes only the embedding layer and output layer
questions.explanation: LoRA freezes all original weights and injects trainable low-rank decomposition matrices (W = W_0 + BA where B is d x r and A is r x d, with r typically 4-64). This means only a tiny fraction of parameters are trainable, dramatically reducing memory requirements and enabling fine-tuning on consumer GPUs. The adapter weights are also very small to store and can be swapped efficiently.

questions.question: What effect does lowering the temperature parameter have during LLM inference?
options: It makes the output longer
It makes the probability distribution sharper, favoring higher-probability tokens and producing more deterministic, focused output
It increases the vocabulary size considered
It speeds up token generation
questions.explanation: Temperature scales the logits before softmax: P(x_i) = exp(z_i/T) / sum(exp(z_j/T)). Lower T makes the distribution peakier -- the highest-probability token gets an even higher probability relative to others. At T->0 (greedy decoding), the model always picks the most likely token, producing deterministic but potentially repetitive output.

questions.question: How does top-p (nucleus) sampling differ from top-k sampling?
options: Top-p is faster to compute than top-k
Top-p keeps a fixed number of tokens while top-k uses a probability threshold
Top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p, adapting the number of candidates based on the model's confidence
Top-p only works with temperature=1.0
questions.explanation: Top-k always considers exactly k tokens regardless of their probability distribution. Top-p adapts: when the model is confident (one token has 95% probability), it might consider only 1-2 tokens; when uncertain, it might consider hundreds. This adaptive behavior makes top-p generally more robust across different contexts.

questions.question: What is the KV cache optimization in transformer inference?
options: It caches the training data to avoid re-reading from disk
It stores the key and value matrices from previous positions so they don't need to be recomputed when generating each new token
It compresses the model weights to use less memory
It pre-computes all possible next tokens
questions.explanation: During autoregressive generation, each new token needs to attend to all previous tokens. Without caching, this requires recomputing Q, K, V for ALL positions at every step. The KV cache stores the K and V matrices from all previous positions, so only the new token's Q, K, V need to be computed. This dramatically reduces computation at the cost of memory that grows linearly with sequence length.
